extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, natural philosophers, and scientists interested in composing or understanding a general physical description of the universe (cosmography)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and methodological guidance for composing a general physical description of the universe — how to balance observation and speculation, choose an ordering and level of detail, and privilege quantitative measurement and careful classification. Focuses on presentation (exposition) of known facts and on the scientific methods that make such a delineation trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between experiment and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The results yielded by an earnest investigation in the path of experiment can not be at variance with a true philosophy of nature. If there be any contradiction, the fault must lie either in the unsoundness of speculation, or in the exaggerated pretensions of empiricism...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental results and speculative theory should be coherent; apparent contradictions indicate either poor theorizing or over-interpretation of experiments. Do not accept experiments as proving more than can be logically derived; seek reconciliation by revising speculation or reassessing empirical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject experimental results to rational combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Science does not present itself to man until mind conquers matter in striving to subject the result of experimental investigation to rational combinations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raw sensory data become science only when the mind arranges them into rational, inductive structures. Emphasize intellectual synthesis (reason and induction) following observation rather than treating observation alone as scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate mind and external nature (avoid strict separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The external world has no real existence for us beyond the image reflected within ourselves through the medium of the senses... The objective world, conceived and reflected within us by thought, is subjected to the eternal and necessary conditions of our intellectual being.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the interplay between perception, language, and thought when describing nature; scientific depiction must account for human cognitive conditions and not treat phenomena as wholly independent of intellectual framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value both austere reason and imaginative speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: “It would be a denial of the dignity of human nature... were we to condemn at one time austere reason engaged in investigating causes and their natural connections, and at another that exercise of the imagination which prompts and excites discoveries by its creative powers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance strict logical/inductive inquiry with imaginative generalization; do not dismiss broad speculative thought when it stimulates hypotheses and discovery, nor privilege imagination at the cost of rigorous testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist excessive detail; avoid endless division in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The descriptive picture of nature which we purpose drawing must not enter too fully into detail... The delineator of nature must resist the tendency toward endless division, in order to avoid the dangers presented by the very abundance of our empirical knowledge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a general delineation prioritize unity and the depiction of major masses or themes rather than exhaustive enumeration of all organisms or processes. Choose granularity that serves the overall picture and prevents the reader from being overwhelmed by minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mean numerical values and quantitative measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: “In all that is subject to motion and change in space, the ultimate aim, the very expression of physical laws, depend upon 'mean numerical values'... the progress of modern physical science is especially characterized by the attainment and rectification of the mean values of certain quantities by means of the processes of weighing and measuring.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize quantitative relations derived from careful measurement (means, averages, magnitudes) as central to expressing physical laws. Where possible, reduce phenomena to measured numbers rather than relying solely on qualitative description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method according to purpose: exposition vs demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: “Another course of ideas must, however, be pursued in a work which proposes merely to give an exposition of what is known... and does not enter into a consideration of the proofs on which such results have been based... The one enumerates what the other demonstrates.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work's aim is to present the current state of knowledge (exposition) or to prove/establish new conclusions (demonstration). For exposition, selection and ordering of known facts (possibly beginning with space) may be appropriate; for conclusive work, present proofs and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and scope: for physical cosmography begin with space (or choose ordering to fit aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A physical cosmography... does not begin, therefore, with the terrestrial, but with that which fills the regions of space... As the sphere of contemplation contracts... our perception of the richness of individual parts becomes enlarged.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a universal physical description, one valid strategy is to start from the remotest regions of space and descend to Earth, thereby situating Earth within a broader cosmic context; alternative orderings are acceptable if they better serve the intended audience or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base knowledge on sensory observation extended by instruments; acknowledge instrument limits
rubrics_metrics.description: “Man learns to know the external world through the organs of the senses. Phenomena of light proclaim the existence of matter in remotest space... The discovery of telescopic vision... has transmitted to latest generations a power whose limits are as yet unattained.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground descriptions on sensory data enhanced by instruments (telescopes etc.), but always remain aware of the instruments' limitations and the continuing extension of observational reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution about historical observational claims (instrument/atmosphere variability)
rubrics_metrics.description: On claiming observed changes in nebulae: “But want of uniformity in the power of the instruments employed, different conditions of our atmosphere, and other optical relations, render a part of the results invalid as historical evidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reports of change over time with skepticism unless observations come from consistent, comparable instruments and viewing conditions; control for instrumental and atmospheric variability before accepting historical changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify astronomical phenomena precisely (taxonomic rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Nebulous stars' must not be confounded either with irregularly-shaped nebulous spots... nor with the so-called planetary nebulae... 'Nebulous stars' are not merely accidental bodies projected upon a nebulous ground, but are a part of the nebulous matter constituting one mass...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain careful, operational definitions and distinctions when classifying observed phenomena (e.g., nebulous stars vs. planetary nebulae vs. irregular nebulous spots); use optical and intensity considerations to differentiate types and avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use uniform counting methods (sidereal scales) to infer spatial distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: “This position of our solar system... have been inferred from sidereal scales, that is to say, from that method of counting the stars ... based upon the equidistant subdivision of the telescopic field of view... These divisions give the length of the ray of vision...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ consistent, repeatable methods (e.g., equidistant subdivisions of telescopic fields and star counts) to infer large-scale distribution and structure; analogize counts to a plummet measuring depth—methodological consistency is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report measurement uncertainty and probable errors
rubrics_metrics.description: References to parallax determinations and 'probable mean error' (e.g., Bessel's and Maclear's parallax work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numerical results together with estimates of probable errors or mean error; acknowledge measurement uncertainty when drawing inferences about distances or distributions.
